title.en: Angulimala, the Robber with the Garland of Fingers

region.zh: 舍衛城郊大道、祇園精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The robber Angulimala, who had worn a garland of his victims' fingers, stalked the Buddha walking alone down the haunted road, yet could not catch him, and at the riddle 'I stand still' he threw his sword into the chasm and was ordained. King Pasenadi came out with five hundred horse to hunt him and found him a yellow-robed elder. later, pelted with clods and stones on his alms-round, he bore the first installment of karma that might have burned him in hell for thousands of years.
summary.zh: 戴人指鬘的劫匪安古利馬拉在凶路上追趕獨行的佛陀，卻怎麼也追不上；在「我已止息」之謎前棄劍懺悔出家。波斯匿王率五百騎出城緝捕，見到的卻是披黃衣的尊者。後來他托缽時被擲石塊土坷，血流破缽，佛陀教他安忍：此是地獄數千年苦報的先付。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely. Contains a serial killer's conversion.

passages.text: In the realm of Pasenadi Kosala lived the robber Finger-Garland, Angulimala, so merciless that villages he harried were villages no more and towns towns no more, and he slew man after man and wore their fingers as a garland. Herdsmen and farmers ran three times to warn the Buddha walking alone into that road, and three times he went on in silence. Angulimala saw him coming and thought to deprive this single unaccompanied monk of life; but though he ran with all his might while the Buddha walked at his usual gait, he could not close the distance. 'Stand still, monk!' he cried. 'I stand still, Angulimala; do you also stand still.' Asked how a walking man could claim to stand still, the Buddha answered that he stood steadfast forever, merciful to all living beings, while Angulimala was merciless to living beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 13, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The robber flung sword and weapons over the precipice, prostrated himself, and begged for ordination; the word 'Come, monk!' sufficed. Soon a hue and cry rose at King Pasenadi's palace gate, and the king set out with five hundred horses to subdue the outlaw. At the grove the Buddha asked what he would do if he saw such a man shaven, yellow-robed, abstaining from killing, stealing, and lying. 'We would salute him, seat him, provide for him,' said the king, 'but how could one so wicked be so restrained?' Then the Teacher stretched forth his hand: 'This, mighty king, is Angulimala!' The king's hair stood on end, but on the Buddha's reassurance he honored the elder, marveling that he who could not subdue the robber with rod or sword had been tamed without either.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 13, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: On his alms-round the new elder saw a woman in the agonies of childbirth and pitied how living beings suffer; sent back with a solemn utterance, he spoke over her, 'Since I was born of the Noble Birth I am not conscious of having deliberately deprived any living being of life; if this be true, may health come to you,' and she was delivered in health. In time he won arahatship. But one morning, as he made his unbroken round of Savatthi, one man threw a clod of earth that struck his body, another a stick, another a stone, till he came to the Buddha with broken head, streaming blood, broken bowl, and rent mantle. 'Endure, Brahman, endure!' said the Teacher; 'you are suffering here and now the fruit of deeds for which you might have been tormented in hell for many thousands of years.' Whose past misdeeds are covered by good deeds, he later said of him, illumines this world as the moon freed from a cloud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 13, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twin Miracle at the Foot of Ganda's Mango-Tree
title.zh: 健陀芒果樹下之雙神變

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: When Pindola won a suspended sandalwood bowl by flying with a mountain under his foot and was rebuked, the heretics challenged the Buddha to out-miracle them; he named the full-moon day, four months off at Savatthi, and they pursued him the whole way. There he sprang a mango-tree from a seed at the gardener's hand, refused the miracle-offers of his mightiest disciples, and walking a jeweled walk in the sky sent fire and water streaming from every pore of his body before ascending in three strides to preach the Abhidhamma to his mother.
summary.zh: 賓度羅跋羅墮阇飛空取缽遭佛訶責，外道遂向佛陀挑戰神變。佛約定四個月後在舍衛城。屆時他以園丁所供芒果一粒種出大樹，謝絕目犍連、蓮花色等弟子請求代現神變，於寶徑上經行，全身毛孔同時出火出水，展現雙神變，隨後三步跨越雪山至三十三天為母說阿毘達磨三個月。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: A treasurer of Rajagaha suspended a red-sandalwood bowl sixty cubits in the air and proclaimed that whoever flew up to take it should make a disciple of him. Six rival teachers strove in vain for six days; on the seventh the Elder Pindolabharadvaja, urged by Moggallana, encircled the flat rock three leagues wide with the tip of his foot, raised it like a silk-cotton tuft, and walked seven times about Rajagaha with it, till the terrified citizens hid under winnowing-baskets. He took the bowl filled with sweet foods; the Teacher rebuked him, had the bowl ground to sandal-paste, and forbade his disciples to work wonders for trifles. The heretics proclaimed that Gotama had banned miracles, and would now perform them with him; the Buddha answered that as a king alone may eat the fruit of his own garden, so the precept bound his disciples but not himself, and named the full-moon of Asalhi, four months hence, near Savatthi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 14, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The heretics pursued him town by town the whole four months, crying that he was running away, and a multitude followed to see. At Savatthi on the appointed day the gardener Ganda offered the Teacher a ripe mango meant for the king; the Buddha drank its sherbet, had the seed planted, washed his hands over it, and instantly a mango-tree fifty cubits high stood there with fruit on one branch, known ever after as Ganda's Mango-tree, while Sakka's winds tore up the heretics' pavilion, scorched and drenched them, and drove the heretic leader Purana to drown himself. Before the miracle, disciples begged to perform it: Gharami would turn the earth to water, Culla Anathapindika would thunder as Maha Brahma, the novice Cira would carry Mount Sineru, Moggallana would crunch Sineru between his teeth and walk the air holding the earth like an umbrella; the nun Uppalavanna would approach as a Universal Monarch. 'I know your power,' said the Teacher to each; 'but this basket of flowers was not prepared for you. My burden is like none other's.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 14, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then before a company thirty-six leagues wide the Teacher performed the Twin Miracle: flames of fire streamed from the upper part of his body and water from the lower, then the reverse; fire and water poured from right and left eyes, ears, nostrils, shoulders, hands, sides, feet, and every pore of his body, in six colors, arching each world-system, while a counterpart of himself walked, stood, sat, or lay opposite him as he moved. Preaching between wonders, he read the heart of everyone in the multitude. Then, as past Buddhas had done, he rose in three strides, mountains huddling under his feet, sixty-eight hundred thousand leagues, to the Yellowstone Throne in the World of the Thirty-three, and for the three months of the rains expounded the Abhidhamma Pitaka to his mother, come down from the Palace of the Tusita gods, while the multitude camped below and Moggallana preached and Culla Anathapindika fed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 14, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Mara Possesses the Villagers and the Buddha Feasts on Joy
title.zh: 魔附村民，佛以法喜為食

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Mara took possession of every body in the Brahman village of Pancasala, so that the Buddha's bowl came out clean as if washed, without a spoonful of rice. Mocked at the gate and told to enter the village again, the Teacher answered that though he received nothing today he would spend the day in the bliss of joy, like the Bright Gods, and spoke the stanza on living happily possessing nothing.
summary.zh: 魔王附身五沙門村全村之人，佛陀托缽一勺飯也未得，缽空如洗。魔羅在村口譏嘲並勸他再入村，欲令村人拍手訕笑。佛陀答：今日雖無所得，我仍將住於法喜之樂，如光音天人般自在，並誦出「無所有而快樂住」一偈。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: The Teacher, perceiving that five hundred maidens of the Brahman village of Pancasala had the faculties for conversion, took up his residence nearby. On a festival day the maidens bathed in the river, adorned themselves with rich apparel and jewels, and set out for the village, and the Teacher entered it on his alms-round. But Mara took possession of the bodies of all the inhabitants, with the result that the Teacher received not so much as a spoonful of boiled rice. As he left with his bowl clean as if just washed, Mara stood at the gate and asked, 'Monk, you received no alms?' 'Embodiment of evil, why have you so wrought that I should receive no alms?' 'Very well, Reverend Sir, enter the village again,' said Mara, planning to make the possessed villagers clap their hands, laugh in his face, and mock him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 15, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that moment the five hundred maidens reached the gate, saluted the Teacher, and stood respectfully on one side. Mara pressed his point: seeing that he had not received a morsel, he must be oppressed with the pangs of hunger. The Teacher answered that embodiment of evil that though today they received nothing, they would spend the day in the bliss of joy, like the Great Brahma in the Heaven of the Bright Gods, and spoke the stanza: Oh, happily let us live, we who possess nothing; let us feed on joy, like the Bright Gods. To possess nothing, and to feast on joy, is the wealth Mara cannot touch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 15, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The King of Kosala Thrice Defeated by His Nephew

region.zh: 憍薩羅國迦西迦村、祇園精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: King Pasenadi of Kosala fought his nephew Ajatasattu near the village of Kasika and was defeated three times, until he took to his bed refusing food, saying there was no use living if he could not subdue that milk-faced youth. The monks reported it, and the Buddha declared that victory breeds hatred and defeat brings suffering, and spoke the stanza on the man who renounces both victory and defeat and lives in tranquillity.
summary.zh: 憍薩羅國波斯匿王在迦西迦村三次敗於其甥阿闍世王，第三敗後不食臥床，嘆不能降此乳色青年便無生趣。比丘們禀告佛陀，佛說勝者生怨恨、敗者受苦惱，捨勝與敗者安樂寂靜。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: The king of Kosala fought against his nephew Ajatasattu near the village of Kasika and suffered defeat three times. Returning from the third defeat he reasoned that since he had not been able to subdue this milk-faced youth, there was no use in his living any longer; so he refused food and took to his bed. The news spread through city and monastery, and the monks told the Teacher that the king, thrice defeated near Kasika, had refused to eat and taken to his bed in despair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 15, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Buddha answered that by winning a victory a man produces hatred, and he that is defeated is afflicted with suffering; only he that renounces both victory and defeat lives in tranquillity and happiness, and spoke the stanza. Hatred need not wait for the battlefield: every victory plants it, and every defeat feeds it; the king's cure lay not in a fourth battle but in laying both aside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 15, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: How Anger Marred the Maiden Rohini's Looks
title.zh: 瞋心毀容的少女羅希尼

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Rohini, sister of the Elder Anuruddha, hid her eruption-covered face behind a cloth until the elder made her spend her jewels on an assembly-hall for the monks; as she swept it her skin cleared. The Buddha traced the eruption to a past life when she, a jealous queen, had powdered scabs secretly into a dancing-girl's bed; anger or jealousy, however slight, is always unbecoming, and Rohini, converted, took on a golden hue and after death was reborn a nymph at whose beauty four deities quarreled.
summary.zh: 阿那律尊者之妹羅希尼因皮膚病以布蒙面，尊者命她傾首飾為僧建講堂；她日日灑掃，瘡疤漸癒。佛陀說其病因：過去為妒后，將瘡痂粉末偷偷撒入舞女的床鋪衣衾，令其潰爛。嫉妒與瞋怒再小也不可取。羅希尼證初果，身現金色，死後生三十三天，四天王為她爭執。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: When the Elder Anuruddha came to Kapilavatthu with five hundred monks, every kinsman paid him respect except his sister Rohini, who stayed at home, ashamed of an eruption of the skin. Summoned, she came with a cloth bound over her face, and the elder asked whether she ought not to perform some work of merit. Told to spend her set of jewels worth ten thousand on building an assembly-hall, she asked who would build it; 'This shall be your duty,' he said to the kinsfolk standing near, 'and I shall stay right here.' So a hall two stories high was raised, and Rohini, standing below as soon as the planks were laid, swept it constantly, filled the water-vessels, and saw the monks seated there from day to day. Even as she swept, the eruption subsided.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 17, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the opening feast she was summoned before the Teacher and asked whether she knew why the eruption had broken out. 'Because of anger,' said the Buddha, and told the story: long ago the chief consort of the king of Benares, hating one of the dancing-girls, powdered large ripe scabs and contrived to place the powder in her bed, cloak, and coverlet, sprinkling some on her body as if in fun; the girl's flesh broke out in boils and she went about scratching, suffering harsher pain on her very bed. That chief consort was Rohini. 'Anger or jealousy, however slight, is always unbecoming.' One should put away anger, utterly renounce pride, and overcome every attachment; whoever clings not to name and form is not beset with pain. At the stanza's close Rohini was established in stream-entry, and her body took on a golden hue. Dying, she was reborn at the meeting-point of four deities' boundaries in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, so fair that the four quarreled over her until Sakka claimed her as his darling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 17, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tree-Spirit Who Spared the Monk Who Cut Her Home

region.zh: 阿羅鞞、舍衛城祇園精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A monk of Alavi set out to fell a tree tenanted by a spirit with an infant child; she begged him to spare her home, placed the baby on a branch, and saw him strike off its arm. About to kill him, she remembered that a righteous man's death would damn her and be copied by other spirits, and went weeping to the Buddha instead. He praised her as a charioteer who reins in anger like a speeding chariot, gave her a vacant tree by the Perfumed Chamber, and laid down the precept against injuring plants.
summary.zh: 阿羅鞞比丘欲砍一神樹建舍，樹神抱子哀求，將幼兒放上枝頭，比丘卻失手砍斷其臂。神怒欲殺之，旋念若殺有德者必墮地獄，且群神效仿則僧眾受害，遂泣告佛陀。佛讚其如馭疾馳戰車者善勒怒馬，並賜祇園香室旁空樹為居，製定不傷草木之戒。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: When the Teacher permitted the monks to lodge outside the monastery walls, a certain monk of Alavi decided to build himself a lodging, and seeing a tree that suited him began to cut it down. A spirit reborn in that tree, carrying her infant child on her hip, appeared before him and begged him not to cut down her home, for she could not wander homeless with her child. 'I shall not be able to find another tree like this,' said the monk, and paid no further heed. The spirit thought that if he only saw the child he would desist, and placed the baby on a branch; but the monk's axe had already swung and could not be checked, and he cut off the child's arm. Furious, the tree-spirit raised both her hands, crying that she would strike him dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 17, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: In an instant another thought came to her: this monk is a righteous man; if she killed him she would go to hell, and if other tree-spirits saw monks cutting down their trees they would imitate her and kill other monks; moreover this monk has a master. Lowering her hands, she went weeping to the Teacher and told him all. 'Well done, well done, spirit!' said the Buddha; 'you have done well in holding in, like a swift-speeding chariot, your anger when it was thus aroused,' and spoke the stanza: whoever controls his anger when it is aroused, like a speeding chariot, him I call a charioteer; other folk merely hold the reins. Though she had won the Fruit of Conversion she stood weeping for her destroyed home, and the Teacher pointed out a tree near the Perfumed Chamber at Jetavana from which a spirit had just departed, telling her to enter it; thereafter no powerful spirit could shake that tree, for its tenant held her abode as a gift from the Buddha. On this occasion the Teacher laid down the observance of the precept regarding the injuring of plants and trees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 17, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Pothila the Empty-Head and the Seven-Year-Old Teacher
title.zh: 波吒拉「空頭」與七歲小老師

region.en: Jetavana; forest hermitage a hundred leagues away
region.zh: 祇園精舍、百里外森林精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Pothila, 'Versed in the Tipitaka' through the dispensations of seven Buddhas, was stung when the Teacher always called him Tucchapothila, the empty-head, and set out to meditate. In a hermitage of thirty arahats the monks passed him down from senior to junior until he stood before a seven-year-old novice, who made him plunge robes and all into a pool to prove his tractability, then taught him to stop five of the six sense-doors and watch the mind's door, whereby the Buddha's image from a hundred leagues away brought him to arahatship.
summary.zh: 經七佛之世皆稱「通三藏」的波吒拉，被佛陀屢喚「空頭波吒拉」所激，前往禪修。三十位阿羅漢將他從上座一路推向最年幼的七歲沙彌。沙彌命他連衣入池以試其受教，再教他關閉五根門、專注意門。佛陀從一百二十由旬外放光照拂，以「從禪定生智慧」一偈令其證阿羅漢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Elder Pothila bore the title Versed in the Tipitaka through the dispensations of all Seven Buddhas and recited the Law to five hundred monks. The Teacher, thinking it had not even occurred to him to seek escape from suffering, stirred him by calling him always Tucchapothila, empty-head: come, empty-head; sit, empty-head; empty-head has gone. Pothila reasoned that the Teacher slighted him because he had never developed the trances, and resolved that very evening to enter the forest and meditate. He walked a hundred and twenty leagues to a hermitage where thirty monks dwelt, and asked each to be his refuge; each, knowing himself an arahat and him a proud scholar, sent him to his junior, until at last the whole chain of monks set him before the youngest of all, a seven-year-old novice doing needlework in his day-quarters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 20, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: His pride humbled, Pothila raised clasped hands to the child: 'Good sir, be my refuge.' The novice answered that one of mature age and great learning should rather teach him, but agreed on one condition, that Pothila endure admonition; the monk vowed he would enter fire if told to. So the novice pointed to a pool and bade him plunge in, robes and all, testing whether the owner of costly double robes was tractable; no sooner were the words spoken than Pothila plunged. Then the novice gave him the lizard simile: in an ant-hill with six holes, he who would catch the lizard stops five and watches the sixth. So should you deal with the six doors of the senses: close five, and give your whole attention to the door of the mind. Pothila concentrated on the material body and began to meditate; the Teacher, a hundred and twenty leagues away, surveyed him and sent forth a luminous image that spoke with him, and by the stanza, from meditation springs wisdom and without it wisdom dwindles away, Pothila attained arahatship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 20, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Thou Shalt Surely Die: the Merchant Who Planned a Year of Trade
title.zh: 你必定要死——盤算全年買賣的商人

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The merchant Mahadhana of Benares, flooding-delayed on the far bank with five hundred cartloads of safflower-dyed cloth, resolved to stay the whole rainy season, winter, and summer selling his goods. The Buddha, seeing he had only seven days to live, sent Ananda to warn him; warned, the merchant fed the Congregation for seven days and at the Teacher's thanksgiving attained stream-entry, then died quietly on his bed and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
summary.zh: 波羅奈商人摩訶檀那載五百車胭脂紅衣布，因河水氾濫滯留對岸，決意留住雨季、冬季、夏季售完貨物再走。佛陀見其壽僅餘七日，遣阿難告知。商人驚懼供僧七日，於佛隨喜時證初果，隨後安臥而逝，生兜率天。愚者盤算久住，不知死期將至。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Merchant Great-Wealth, Mahadhana of Benares, loaded five hundred carts with cloth dyed with safflower and set out to trade. Returning toward Savatthi he reached the river bank and thought to cross the morrow; that night a storm burst, and for seven days the river was at flood while the citizens kept holiday, so that he found no chance to sell his crimson cloths. He reasoned that to go back would mean delay, and resolved to dwell right there through the rainy season, the winter, and the summer, doing his work and selling his goods. As the Teacher made his alms-pilgrimage through the city he became aware of the intention and smiled, telling Ananda that not realizing the end of his life was near, the merchant had made up his mind to stay a whole year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 20, story 10 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Only seven days longer will he live,' said the Buddha, and bade Ananda warn him. The elder made his alms-round at the cart-enclosure, was fed, and asked how long the merchant meant to stay; told a whole year, he answered that though the end of life be near, it is hard to realize, and that only seven days more remained. Overcome, the merchant invited the Congregation with the Buddha, gave alms seven days, and on the last took the Teacher's bowl to receive the words of thanksgiving. 'A wise man,' said the Teacher, 'should never allow himself to think, Right here will I dwell during the rain, during the winter and summer; I will do this work and that. Here will I dwell through the rains, the simpleton imagines, knowing not that he must die.' At the lesson's close the merchant was established in the Fruit of Conversion. He walked a little way with the Teacher, complained of a trouble in his head, lay down on his bed, and no sooner had he lain down than he died, and was reborn in the World of the Tusita gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 20, story 10 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ascent of the Ganges and the Jewel Sutta

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Vesali, stricken by famine, evil spirits, and pestilence, sent for the Buddha; he crossed the Ganges on a jeweled float while Bimbisara waded neck-deep behind it, and at the city gate Ananda recited the Jewel Sutta, drops of silver water falling on the sick and curing them as the spirits fled through walls. Naga kings, deities, and kings covered the river with parasols and lotuses, and the Buddha explained it all as the fruit of one slight offering of grass, sand, and flowers he once made at a Private Buddha's shrine.
summary.zh: 毗舍離遭飢荒、惡鬼、疫病三災，遣使請佛。頻毘娑羅王鋪路五由旬送佛至河，以珠寶浮舟渡河；佛陀一登岸大雨傾盆，屍骸盡沖入河，大地清淨。阿難持缽誦《寶經》繞城三匝，水珠如銀丸落於病者身上，疫病隨愈，惡鬼破牆而逃。天、龍、王傘蓋蓮花滿河；佛說此皆過去於辟支佛塔前拔草、鋪沙、撒花之小施所感。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: When Vesali's crops failed, corpses drew evil spirits, the spirits brought intestinal disease, and three plagues wasted the city, the Licchavi assembly, finding no fault in their king, resolved to send for the Buddha. Mahali obtained Bimbisara's leave, and the king smoothed a five-league road to the Ganges with rest-houses each league and flowers knee-deep, conducting the Teacher in five days. On a jeweled float the Buddha crossed the boundary of Vesali's territory, the king wading behind the float to his neck in promise, 'Until the Exalted One returns, I shall remain right here on the bank of the Ganges.' The Licchavi princes, meeting him in the water, doubled the king's honors; the moment the Teacher set foot ashore a storm burst, washing every corpse into the Ganges and leaving the region pure and sweet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 21, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sakka drew near with his deities and most of the evil spirits fled. At the gate of the city the Teacher gave Ananda the Jewel Sutta to recite as a protection within the three walls, making the rounds with the Licchavi princes. When Ananda uttered the word 'Whatsoever' and threw water upward from the stone bowl, it fell upon the sick and cured them where they stood, while drops like balls of silver fell upon the evil spirits, who strove to escape by every door and, finding not room enough in a thousand doors, broke down the walls and fled. In the town-hall the Teacher recited the Jewel Sutta again, and eighty-four thousand beings obtained comprehension of the Law; for seven days the plague abated, and he departed, honored on the river by Naga kings with boats of gold and silver and by deities from earth to the Brahma world with parasol after parasol, while he created a counterfeit Buddha in each boat, one festival within the whole circle of the Cakkavala.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 21, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The monks marveled that such honor had come from Buddha-power or from nagas, deities, and Brahma; the Buddha corrected them: it came from a slight offering made in a previous existence. Long ago the Brahman Sankha of Takshashila, seeking his son Susima, found that the youth had become a Private Buddha at Isipatana, passed into Nibbana quickly, and been enshrined at the gate of Benares. The father wept, then tore up the grass in the shrine's enclosure, brought sand in his outer garment and spread it, sprinkled the ground with water from his pot, scattered wild flowers, raised his robe as a banner, and planted his own parasol over the mound. 'It was I who uprooted that grass,' said the Buddha; 'as its fruit these princes cleared a road eight leagues long. I spread the sand, and they spread sand; I scattered flowers, and lotuses of five colors covered the Ganges a league; I sprinkled water, and a shower fell on Vesali; I raised a banner and planted a parasol, and parasols rose as far as the highest heaven.' If by renouncing some trifling pleasure one may obtain pleasure abounding, a wise man renounces the trifling pleasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 21, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Young Archer the Wise and the Wife Who Bartered Husbands

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A young monk grown yellow with longing for a householder's wife was told by the Buddha of his own past life as Young Archer the Wise, who slew fifty bandits with fifty arrows and yet was killed by the bandit his wife had fallen for; the bandit himself abandoned her by a river, and Sakka, as a jackal that lost both fish and flesh, shamed her. Doubt agitated and passion swaying him strengthen the bond; meditating on the unlovely cleaves it.
summary.zh: 年輕比丘因思念施主之女而面黃肌瘦。佛陀說過去世他為智箭少年，五十箭射殺五十盜，其妻卻瞬間愛上倖存盜首、遞劍害夫；盜首懼她移情，渡河棄她而去。帝釋化為失魚失肉的胡狼譏其更慘，她自慚形穢。佛陀教他：疑惱與貪愛只會加固魔縛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: A young monk who went for drinking-water to a certain house fell in love with the young woman there; she fed him rice-gruel, then boiled rice, and talked to him of how lonely the house was, until he grew yellow with discontent. Taken to the Teacher, he confessed the cause, and the Buddha told him it was no strange thing for such a woman to act so: in a previous existence she forsook Dhanuggaha, the wisest man in all India, conceived a sudden passion for a bandit, and slew her husband. In times past Young Archer the Wise, trained at Takshashila and married to his teacher's daughter, was set on at the forest's entrance by fifty bandits and slew them all with fifty arrows; when the arrows were gone he seized the leader, and 'Wife, bring me my sword!' But the moment she saw the bandit she conceived a passion for him, and set the sword's hilt in the bandit's hand, and he slew Young Archer the Wise and took her away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 24, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Going on his way, the bandit reasoned that a woman who could betray one husband would kill him too, and at a river left her on the near bank, 'Remain until I carry your ornaments across,' and crossed alone, taking everything. 'You have taken all my ornaments and crossed,' she cried; 'return speedily, now take me too.' 'Woman,' he answered, 'you bartered a husband long known for one unknown; you may barter me for another man. Therefore I will go far from hence.' Then Sakka came to put her to shame, as a jackal with a piece of meat, his charioteer a fish, his musician a bird: the jackal sprang at the leaping fish, dropped the meat, and the bird snatched it into the air, so the jackal lost both fish and flesh and mourned like a pauper. The woman laughed; the jackal retorted that easy to see are the faults of others, hard to see one's own: she had lost both husband and lover, and would do evil again. The wisest man in India was Young Archer; the jackal was the Buddha himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 24, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Monk, uproot and destroy the desire which has sprung up within you for this woman,' said the Teacher, and expounded the two stanzas: if a man be agitated by doubt, swayed by strong passion, seeking only what is pleasing, craving increases the more, and he strengthens the bond that holds him; but whoever delights in suppressing doubt and meditates with mindfulness on what is not pleasing will destroy and cleave the bond of Mara. The monk uprooted his desire, and the wife's fickleness stood revealed as the very shape of craving.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 24, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Uggasena the Tumbler Converts on the Tip of the Pole
title.zh: 烏迦西那——竿頂當下轉法

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A treasurer's son fell in love with a tumbler's daughter and followed her troupe as a cart-driver, enduring his wife's contempt until he mastered tumbling himself. Announced to perform in Rajagaha, he balanced on a sixty-cubit pole just as the Buddha entered the city and every eye turned away; when the Teacher asked him to perform anyway, the youth turned fourteen somersaults and heard the stanza on giving up past, present, and future, and won arahatship balanced on the pole's tip.
summary.zh: 長者之子愛上賣藝女子，入班隨行拉車燒水，妻子譏他「車夫之子」。他憤而學藝，一年練成，預告七日後於王舍城表演。佛陀恰於其登竿之時入城，萬眾目光全被佛奪。目犍連受命請他表演，他連翻十四個觔斗，佛陀說偈教其放下過去、現在、未來，他在竿頂證阿羅漢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Twice a year five hundred tumblers gave seven days of performances at Rajagaha, and a certain treasurer's son, watching from a pile of beds, fell in love with a tumbler's daughter balancing on the tip of a pole. 'If I can have her I shall live; if not, I will die right here,' he told his parents, refusing all food and every better-bred bride. The tumbler would take no money, but promised the girl if the young man would travel with the troupe; so the treasurer's son became a cart-driver, fetching grass for the oxen and setting up the apparatus, while his wife sang to their baby son of 'the son of a cart-driver, the son of a know-nothing.' Told she meant him, he set out to learn her art, mastered every feat his father-in-law knew, and had it proclaimed through Rajagaha that seven days hence Uggasena the treasurer's son would exhibit his skill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 24, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the seventh day he climbed a pole sixty cubits high and balanced on its tip, while the city raised platform upon platform. The Teacher, who saw that Uggasena had entered the Net of his Knowledge and would win arahatship that day before breakfast, timed his entry into the city to the moment, and every eye turned from the performer to the Buddha. Uggasena, perceiving the crowd no longer looked at him, felt his year of labor wasted; and the Teacher, reading the thought, sent Moggallana to cry, 'Pray look, Uggasena, tumbler of mighty strength; perform for the crowd.' Delighted, the youth answered the elder in verse, sprang from the pole, turned fourteen somersaults in the air, and lit again on the tip. 'A wise man,' said the Buddha, 'should put away attachment for the elements of being in the past, the present, and the future: give up the things of the future, give up the things of the past, give up the things of the present; cross to the Farther Shore.' Eighty-four thousand beings understood the Law, and Uggasena, balanced on the pole's tip, attained arahatship, descended, and was ordained with the word 'Come, monk!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 24, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked afterwards whether he had felt no fear descending from that pole, Uggasena said he had none, and the monks thought he lied, until the Teacher said those who, like his son, have severed the attachments have no fear: he that has severed every attachment and trembles not, him I call a Brahman. The Buddha explained both the troupe-life and the swift attainment by one past circumstance: while the golden shrine of Kassapa Buddha was building, a young wife seeing an elder pass for alms filled his bowl from her family's loaded cart, and both husband and wife wished to share the truth he had seen; the elder arahat smiled, and she said, 'Our noble elder smiled; he must be some actor.' 'He must indeed, my dear wife,' her husband agreed. Because of that answer he traveled with actors; because of the food given an arahat he attained arahatship; and his wife, vowing to reach whatever estate he reached, left the world and won the same.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 24, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Mahapajapati Gotami Receives the Eight Cardinal Precepts
title.zh: 大愛道瞿曇彌受八尊法

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Mahapajapati Gotami, the Buddha's foster-mother, was admitted to full membership in the Order by the Eight Cardinal Precepts, which she accepted from the Buddha's own mouth by bowing her head, as one accustomed to ornaments accepts a garland, having no teacher or preceptor but him. When her retinue spread the report and other nuns refused to keep fast-day with her, the Buddha confirmed that he alone was her teacher, and preached that he who offends not by act, speech, or thought is a Brahman.
summary.zh: 佛陀養母大愛道瞿曇彌受八尊法而得具足戒，如戴慣瓔珞之人低頭受花鬘，無導師和尚，唯以佛為師。諸比丘尼聽信謠言，不肯與她共布薩、共自恣。佛陀明言：八尊法乃我親授，我即是她的導師與和尚。身口意無過者，我稱之為婆羅門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Previous to the public promulgation of the Eight Cardinal Precepts, the Exalted One proclaimed them privately, and Mahapajapati Gotami accepted them by bowing her head, just as a person accustomed to the wearing of ornaments accepts a garland of fragrant flowers by bowing his head; so did all the members of her retinue. No preceptor or teacher did she have other than the Exalted One himself, and thus she received admission to full membership in the Order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 26, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: On a later occasion members of her retinue remarked that the great nun had no teacher or preceptor, but had received the yellow robes by herself alone and with her own hand; the other nuns, hearing it, were dissatisfied and thenceforth refused to keep the fast-day or celebrate the terminal festival with her, and reported the matter to the Tathagata. The Teacher answered that he himself had conferred the Eight Cardinal Precepts on Mahapajapati Gotami, that he alone was her teacher and he alone her preceptor, and that those who have renounced the sins of act and speech and thought, and rid themselves of the evil passions, should never entertain feelings of dissatisfaction. He that offends not by act or speech or thought, and controls himself in these three respects, that man I call a Brahman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 26, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Sivali, Seven Years in the Womb

region.zh: 恭達憍利附近之恭達達那園

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Suppavasa of the Koliya clan carried a child in her womb for seven years and lay seven days in bitter pains, reflecting on the Buddha, the Order that walks in righteousness, and the Nibbana where such suffering is no more. Sent for, the Teacher pronounced a benediction and the healthy boy was born at once; mother and son fed the Congregation for seven days, the boy strained water for the monks from birth, grew up to win arahatship, and was comforted by the stanza on him who has crossed the quagmire of rebirth.
summary.zh: 拘利族女須婆瓦薩懷胎七年，臨盆劇痛七日，她憶念佛陀、正道而行之僧團，與此苦不復存在之涅槃，以三念忍受。丈夫奉命請佛，佛一句祝願，她隨即平安產下健康男嬰。母子七日供僧，嬰兒自出生即為僧眾濾水，長大出家證阿羅漢。佛以「渡過此難渡之泥沼者」一偈慰之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Once upon a time Suppavasa, a daughter of the Koliya clan, carried a child in her womb for seven years; and for seven days, since the child lay awry, she was stricken with distressing, acute, and bitter pains. In her torment she reflected that supremely Enlightened, truly, was the Exalted One who preached a religion for the putting away of suffering such as this; that walking in righteousness, truly, was the Order of that Exalted One, which walks in righteousness to the putting away of suffering such as this; and that blessed, truly, was Nibbana, where suffering such as this exists no more. With these three reflections she endured the pain, and sent her husband to greet the Teacher in her name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 26, story 31 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the husband had conveyed her message the Teacher said, 'May Suppavasa, the young woman of the Koliya clan, be healthy; in health and happiness may she bring forth a healthy son,' and the moment the words were uttered Suppavasa brought forth a healthy son in health and happiness. Forthwith she invited the Congregation of Monks presided over by the Buddha, and for seven days gave bountiful offerings; and from the day of his birth her son took a strainer-fitted water-pot and strained water for the Congregation of Monks. In time he retired from the world, became a monk, and attained arahatship. When the monks marvelled in the Hall of Truth that so illustrious a monk had endured such suffering in the womb, the Teacher said that his son had now obtained release from all that suffering and abode in the bliss of Nibbana: whoever has crossed this quagmire, difficult to cross, rebirth, delusion, whoever has gained the other shore, devoted to meditation, free from lust, doubt, and craving, tranquil, such a man I call a Brahman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 26, story 31 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.
